title: A multicentre comparative study of health sciences students' preferences for instructors' nonverbal communication skills across participating universities in Saudi Arabia and Malaysia
content:
by Raju Suresh Kumar, Shinu Pottathil, M.Ganesh Kamath, Muhammad Anwar Khan, Ahmaed Baashar, Abdulaziz Saleh Almulhim, Krutika Darbar Shaikh, Anroop B. Nair, Rekha Prabhu, Afzal Haq Asif, Hussien Yahya Almutawa, Abdullah Abdulhamid Ahmed Altaweel

Nonverbal communication (NVC) is an important component of instructor–student interaction, yet evidence regarding health professions students’ perceptions across different educational and cultural settings remains limited. This multicentre cross-sectional study examined students’ perceptions of instructors’ NVC and explored the psychometric properties of a researcher-developed questionnaire across three universities in Saudi Arabia and Malaysia. Undergraduate health professions students completed a 21-item, five-point Likert-scale questionnaire. Psychometric evaluation included exploratory factor analysis, parallel analysis, internal consistency assessment, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Factor-derived composite scores were subsequently examined using multivariable linear regression with robust standard errors. Among 723 participants (mean age 20.1 ± 1.45 years; 64.3% female), exploratory analyses supported two domains: Instructor Expressiveness and Classroom Engagement (Domain 1) and Instructor Physical Presence and Lecture Delivery Style (Domain 2). Internal consistency was good for the overall questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.838) and Domain 1 (α = 0.869), but lower for Domain 2 (α = 0.694). CFA did not demonstrate satisfactory model fit, indicating that the identified domains remain exploratory. Students generally reported favourable perceptions of instructors’ NVC. In adjusted analyses, male gender was associated with higher Domain 2 scores (β = 0.215, 95% CI 0.059–0.372, P = 0.007), as was increasing age (β = 0.063, 95% CI 0.019–0.106, P = 0.005). Country was not independently associated with either domain, and no significant country-by-gender interactions were identified. These findings suggest broadly similar perceptions of instructor NVC across the participating settings but do not establish cultural equivalence or teaching outcomes. Further refinement and independent validation of the questionnaire, including measurement invariance testing, are required before broader application.
